Today, Ali Lyon, assesses whether August’s positive GDP figures are a sign of a revival in the UK economy. Sign up to the City AM News Updates newsletter here.For much of the past decade and a half, describing the UK economy has been a relatively easy task.

‘Languid’ has often worked. ‘Stuttering’ has been another favourite. And when things have looked especially sullen, ‘moribund’ or ‘anaemic’ have more than sufficed.But if today’s GDP figures are anything to go by, then cliche-dependent hacks like this one might find themselves having to reach for their thesauruses in search of a new vernacular.Granted, a 0.1 per cent jump in economic activity in August is hardly cause to crack open the English sparkling wine.
But it was, as almost every economist has been at pains to point out this morning, an expectation-defying 0.1 per cent nevertheless.The headwinds facing the upward nudge were manifold.
And the sources of that resilience – improved productivity, early signs of a tech boom, and an uptick in our, yes, ‘moribund’ manufacturing sector – inspire some confidence.

articles.headline: They asked for 80 homes – she gave them 157! Council-housing miracle named Britain’s best new building
articles.dek: Rising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prize If Andy Burnham is looking for inspiratio…
articles.lead: Rising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prize If Andy Burnham is looking for inspiration for his great “council housebuilding comeback”, he would do well to visit Croydon.
articles.takeaway: Rising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prize If Andy Burnham is looking for inspiratio…
body: Rising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prize If Andy Burnham is looking for inspiration for his great “council housebuilding comeback”, he would do well to visit Croydon.

There, nestled into a steeply sloping site, sheltered by a canopy of mature trees, stands a cluster of crystalline pink and brown brick towers, where generous flats look on to a landscape of allotments, playgrounds and to the rolling hills of south London beyond.

Designed by Mary Duggan Architects, with Ruff Architects, it is a model of council-led housebuilding – so much so that it has also been named this year’s best building in the UK, confounding the bookies’ outsider odds.

Only once before has the RIBA Stirling prize ever been awarded to a council housing project, when Goldsmith Street in Norwich scooped the gong in 2019, for its rows of low-energy brick terraces, designed by Mikhail Riches Architects and Cathy Hawley.

This year’s winner, Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, is an entirely different animal, and it puts a welcome spotlight back on housing design at a time when the government plans to pump £39bn into the sector.

It is also a bittersweet vindication of Croydon council’s erstwhile housebuilding company, Brick by Brick, a bold and sadly brief experiment by the previous Labour administration, which was halted in 2020 when the council went bankrupt, seeing numerous projects cancelled.

articles.headline: South London Housing Project Wins Prestigious Stirling Prize
articles.dek: Lion Green Road development in Coulsdon recognized by Riba for innovative design and integration into natural landscape.
articles.lead: A housing development in Coulsdon, south London, has been awarded the 2026 Stirling Prize by the Royal Institute of British Architects (Riba). The Lion Green Road project, designed by Mary Duggan Architects and built with RUFF Architects, features 157 homes across five unique 13-sided blocks.
articles.takeaway: Lion Green Road development in Coulsdon recognized by Riba for innovative design and integration into natural landscape.
body: A housing development in Coulsdon, south London, has been awarded the 2026 Stirling Prize by the Royal Institute of British Architects (Riba). The Lion Green Road project, designed by Mary Duggan Architects and built with RUFF Architects, features 157 homes across five unique 13-sided blocks.

The development, which replaces a former car park on a sloping site, was praised by judges for its sensitive integration into the surrounding natural beauty and its "new approach to higher density development." The project combines affordable and private housing for Croydon Council.

Mary Duggan described the project as being "about the culture of dwelling," aiming to create non-institutional housing and rethink what affordable housing can offer communities. The design challenges conventional suburban layouts by incorporating winding paths and planting that weave between the blocks, linking shared outdoor spaces and creating a sense of belonging.

Riba president Chris Williamson highlighted the project's importance in addressing the need for quality housing, noting that many people from similar backgrounds to his own live in inadequate accommodation. The development's soft purple and pink brickwork and its placement among trees on the edge of green-belt land allow it to blend seamlessly into the landscape.

The project was funded by Croydon Council as a public asset and was recognized for its inventive and site-specific response to a constrained plot, considering criteria such as design vision, innovation, sustainability, and functionality.

articles.headline: Lambeth Council Halts Demolition of Two South London Housing Estates
articles.dek: Cressingham Gardens and Central Hill estates, celebrated for their 1960s architecture, are to be saved from demolition following a decade-long campaign by residents.
articles.lead: Lambeth council is set to reverse its plans to demolish the Cressingham Gardens and Central Hill housing estates in south London. The decision follows a decade-long campaign by residents who argued the 1960s developments are architecturally significant and desirable places to live.
articles.takeaway: Cressingham Gardens and Central Hill estates, celebrated for their 1960s architecture, are to be saved from demolition following a decade-long campaign by residents.
body: Lambeth council is set to reverse its plans to demolish the Cressingham Gardens and Central Hill housing estates in south London. The decision follows a decade-long campaign by residents who argued the 1960s developments are architecturally significant and desirable places to live.

The estates, designed by Lambeth architects led by Ted Hollamby, were intended to foster community and move away from tower blocks. Cressingham Gardens was built with features to encourage neighbourliness and play, while Central Hill was designed to maximize light and views on a sloping site.

Previous plans under a Labour-controlled council aimed to replace the estates, citing poor repair and a need for more social and affordable housing. However, a 2022 review of Homes Lambeth, the council's former housing management body, questioned the redevelopment, noting a very small net increase in social rent homes.

The Green party, which now leads the council as a minority administration, has opposed the demolition. The reversal is expected to be confirmed at a cabinet meeting next week. The council now plans to focus on investing in existing homes and bringing empty properties back into use.

Residents and leaseholders had lived in uncertainty for years as demolition plans were pursued. Feedback from residents during the review process was described as uniformly negative, with concerns about inconsistent policy, delays, and poor communication leading to low trust in the council.

articles.headline: Lewisham Council's 1970s Self-Build Housing Project Praised
articles.dek: A pioneering initiative in the 1970s provided materials and guidance for residents to build their own homes, fostering community and pride.
articles.lead: A self-build housing project initiated in the 1970s in Lewisham, London, has been highlighted as a significant success. The scheme, which utilized methods developed by German architect Walter Segal, was spearheaded by Brian Richardson, an architect with Lewisham council at the time.
articles.takeaway: A pioneering initiative in the 1970s provided materials and guidance for residents to build their own homes, fostering community and pride.
body: A self-build housing project initiated in the 1970s in Lewisham, London, has been highlighted as a significant success. The scheme, which utilized methods developed by German architect Walter Segal, was spearheaded by Brian Richardson, an architect with Lewisham council at the time.

Richardson convinced the local authority to provide materials to individuals on the council house waiting list, enabling them to construct their own homes. Participants, who initially lacked building skills, worked during evenings and weekends to erect their houses and establish a community.
Beyond the physical construction, Richardson noted that a key achievement of the project was the positive transformation in the self-builders themselves, boosting their pride and self-confidence.

Contemporary discussions about addressing the UK's housing challenges have revisited this successful model. Lewisham council is again exploring plans to offer publicly owned land for community-led social housing projects.

This approach aims to overcome the barrier of land value, which often hinders the development of social housing, particularly on smaller sites. While challenges in building costs, funding, and planning remain, making land available could unlock smaller, community-driven initiatives.

attribution.originalTitle: Build-it-yourself housing project was a huge success in 1970s Lewisham | Letters

faqs.answer: It was an initiative where Lewisham council provided materials and guidance for residents on the waiting list to build their own homes using Walter Segal's methods.

faqs.answer: It can help reduce land costs, making it more viable for community groups to develop social housing, especially on smaller sites.

articles.headline: Chancellor John Healey Considers Bank Tax Amid Conflicting Signals
articles.dek: The UK's banking sector faces uncertainty as reports emerge of potential tax hikes, contrasting with recent supportive statements from the Chancellor.
articles.lead: Chancellor John Healey is reportedly considering new tax measures targeting the banking industry in the upcoming Budget, a move that has caused consternation among financial sector leaders. The City of London has been left reeling by reports that the Treasury is drawing up plans for a significant tax increase on banks.
articles.takeaway: The UK's banking sector faces uncertainty as reports emerge of potential tax hikes, contrasting with recent supportive statements from the Chancellor.
body: Chancellor John Healey is reportedly considering new tax measures targeting the banking industry in the upcoming Budget, a move that has caused consternation among financial sector leaders. The City of London has been left reeling by reports that the Treasury is drawing up plans for a significant tax increase on banks.

These potential plans come shortly after Healey described banks as "part of the jewel in the British economic crown" and "hardwired into the economic fabric of this country" at an IMF summit. However, he also broadly acknowledged that "decisions to take in the Budget," leaving the sector with mixed messages.

Industry heavyweights have voiced strong opposition, with one City figure calling a bank tax a "retrograde step" that would not align with the Chancellor's recent positive remarks. Concerns have been raised that such a tax would harm the international competitiveness of the UK's financial services, which already face higher tax burdens than in competing financial centers like Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Dublin, and New York.

One potential lever for Healey could be reversing the reduction of the banking surcharge from eight percent to three percent, a move that could raise an estimated £2 billion annually. However, industry bodies like UK Finance have urged the government to maintain tax stability and focus on reforms that enhance the sector's capacity to finance the wider economy, warning that increased taxes would act as a "tax on investment."

articles.headline: London IPOs Hit Lowest Point Since 2023 in Q3
articles.dek: Only one company listed on the London Stock Exchange in the third quarter, marking the quietest period since late 2023, though capital raised saw an increase.
articles.lead: London saw just one Initial Public Offering (IPO) in the third quarter of 2026, the lowest number of listings since 2023. The sole transaction was the AIM listing of 1947 Oil & Gas plc, which raised £29.8m. This marks the quietest period for London listings since the fourth quarter of 2023, when no companies listed.
articles.takeaway: Only one company listed on the London Stock Exchange in the third quarter, marking the quietest period since late 2023, though capital raised saw an increase.
body: London saw just one Initial Public Offering (IPO) in the third quarter of 2026, the lowest number of listings since 2023. The sole transaction was the AIM listing of 1947 Oil & Gas plc, which raised £29.8m. This marks the quietest period for London listings since the fourth quarter of 2023, when no companies listed.

Despite the low volume of new listings, the total capital raised in the third quarter increased significantly compared to the same period in 2025, rising from £199.1m to £5.3bn. This boost was largely due to the debut of African payments firm Airtel Money.

Analysts attribute the slowdown to several factors, including the typical lull in summer activity and broader macroeconomic uncertainty stemming from global conflicts and fiscal policy developments. Many companies are reportedly delaying their IPO plans until 2027, anticipating improved market conditions.

However, potential government decisions in the upcoming Autumn Budget could impact the IPO pipeline. Industry figures are urging the government to abolish the 0.5 per cent stamp duty on UK stocks, which they argue acts as a disincentive to investment.

Globally, the IPO market performed more strongly, with 387 IPOs across international markets in the third quarter, raising $95.6bn. Middle Eastern and African markets, particularly India, led global activity, while European and Asia-Pacific markets also saw significant investor interest in sectors like defence, infrastructure, energy, and AI.

body: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares last year OpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.

Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.

The earnings amount to 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings, according to the Office for National Statistics. An OpenAI worker on an average package could expect to take home about £1,000 an hour in salary and equity before tax.

But there is understood to be a wide discrepancy between the highest and lowest earners. The biggest compensation packages are reserved for AI researchers who help build the San Francisco company’s cutting-edge models such as Astra.
The figures relate to 2025, when there was a talent war and OpenAI’s rival, Meta, was reported to be offering multi-year packages running into several hundred million dollars.

OpenAI’s London base reflects the UK capital’s status as an important hub for AI talent with some of the brightest machine-learning experts and AI researchers coming out of universities such as Cambridge.

articles.headline: Greenwich Council Opposes Charlton Data Centre Proposal Amid Housing Concerns
articles.dek: A proposed 1 million sq ft data centre development in Charlton faces opposition from Greenwich Council, which prioritizes housing and regeneration plans for the area.
articles.lead: Greenwich Council has voiced opposition to a proposed 1 million square foot data centre development on industrial land in Charlton Riverside. The council argues the proposal conflicts with its plans for the area, which include building approximately 8,000 homes, enhancing public transport, and creating 1,000 new jobs.
articles.takeaway: A proposed 1 million sq ft data centre development in Charlton faces opposition from Greenwich Council, which prioritizes housing and regeneration plans for the area.
body: Greenwich Council has voiced opposition to a proposed 1 million square foot data centre development on industrial land in Charlton Riverside. The council argues the proposal conflicts with its plans for the area, which include building approximately 8,000 homes, enhancing public transport, and creating 1,000 new jobs.

The site, currently designated for mixed-use development comprising residential, commercial, and light industrial uses, has become a focal point in the broader debate about land use in London. As demand for digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence grows, data centres are increasingly competing with housing and regeneration ambitions for valuable urban space.

Supporters of data centres emphasize their role as critical infrastructure powering essential digital services. However, critics raise concerns about their significant energy and water consumption, as well as their environmental impact, questioning their suitability for areas earmarked for new housing.

Data centre developers are drawn to London due to its concentration of businesses, financial services, and internet connectivity. The Charlton proposal, if approved, would be situated on the Stone Foundries and VIP trading estates and the CSB Logistics building. A spokesperson for the data centre project stated that regeneration in the area has seen limited progress and highlighted that data centres are designated as Critical National Infrastructure by the government.

Residents have expressed concerns about potential noise from generators and the high energy and water usage of data centres, with many preferring to see new homes built on the site. Data centre operators counter that newer facilities use advanced cooling systems, employ noise-dampening equipment, and that their overall water usage is minimal compared to water lost through leaks in the national supply system.

articles.headline: London's Oldest Restaurant Building Donated to National Trust
articles.dek: The historic home of Rules, established in 1798, has been gifted to the heritage charity to ensure its preservation.
articles.lead: The building housing Rules, London's oldest restaurant, has been donated to the National Trust by its owner, J.P. Mayhew. The gift, valued at £11 million, marks the National Trust's first venture into the restaurant business, though it already manages numerous historic pubs and hotels.
articles.takeaway: The historic home of Rules, established in 1798, has been gifted to the heritage charity to ensure its preservation.
body: The building housing Rules, London's oldest restaurant, has been donated to the National Trust by its owner, J.P. Mayhew. The gift, valued at £11 million, marks the National Trust's first venture into the restaurant business, though it already manages numerous historic pubs and hotels.

Rules, founded in 1798 on Maiden Lane in Covent Garden, has a rich history, having been frequented by notable figures such as Charles Dickens, Laurence Olivier, and Charlie Chaplin. The restaurant's interior, with its playbills, caricatures, and antlers, remains largely unchanged from the 19th century.

While Mayhew has donated the historic building and its contents, the restaurant business itself was sold to its general manager, Ricky McMenemy, in 2022. McMenemy will operate as a commercial tenant of the National Trust.

Lucy Porten of the National Trust stated that the charity's involvement will be light-touch, with the restaurant continuing to operate as a business. The menu will remain largely the same, and there will be no changes for National Trust members, such as preferential access or pricing.

The National Trust plans to explore options for virtual visits to allow people to experience the space remotely. The charity views the restaurant as an opportunity to tell different histories and preserve a significant slice of London's social history.

faqs.answer: The restaurant business at Rules is owned by its longstanding general manager, Ricky McMenemy.

faqs.answer: No, the National Trust has stated that the menu will remain largely the same and will not include items like scones.

articles.headline: Richmond Council Proposes Kew Riverside Primary School Closure
articles.dek: Parents express deep concern over potential closure of Kew Riverside Primary School due to declining student numbers and budget deficits, citing the school's nurturing environment and community impact.
articles.lead: Richmond Council is considering the closure of Kew Riverside Primary School, a decision that parents argue would be devastating to the local community. The school, which has a capacity for 210 students, currently has only 87 pupils, leading to a projected budget deficit of £400,000 by 2028.
articles.takeaway: Parents express deep concern over potential closure of Kew Riverside Primary School due to declining student numbers and budget deficits, citing the school's nurturing environment and community impact.
body: Richmond Council is considering the closure of Kew Riverside Primary School, a decision that parents argue would be devastating to the local community. The school, which has a capacity for 210 students, currently has only 87 pupils, leading to a projected budget deficit of £400,000 by 2028.

Parents have voiced strong opposition to the proposals, highlighting the school's role as a close-knit community and a supportive environment for children, particularly those with special educational needs and disabilities. Iona Ferguson, a parent of a Year Five pupil with SEND, described the school as a "gamechanger" for her child, who has thrived academically and emotionally.

Council leader Gareth Roberts stated that while the proposals are in the consultation phase, the decision is influenced by falling birth rates and significant cuts to core funding. He assured that all students would be offered places at other schools if Kew Riverside were to close, but acknowledged the difficult financial realities.

A Department for Education spokesperson emphasized the government's commitment to ensuring every child has access to a good school place and highlighted increased funding for schools and SEND provision. However, parents are working to demonstrate the school's potential to attract new students and become financially viable, urging the council to consider the impact on families and ensure a fair process.

The potential closure of Kew Riverside Primary School reflects a broader trend in London, where primary school numbers are declining sharply due to factors including the high cost of living, forcing families to move out of the capital. Experts note that declining pupil numbers directly impact school budgets, as funding is tied to student enrollment.

articles.headline: City of London Investment Banks Shift to Shared Infrastructure
articles.dek: Investment banks are moving away from self-operated back-office functions towards collaborative systems to support AI and reduce operational complexity.
articles.lead: Forty years after the Big Bang reforms transformed the City of London into a global electronic marketplace, a new structural shift is underway. This revolution is not occurring on trading floors, but within the essential infrastructure that supports capital markets.
articles.takeaway: Investment banks are moving away from self-operated back-office functions towards collaborative systems to support AI and reduce operational complexity.
body: Forty years after the Big Bang reforms transformed the City of London into a global electronic marketplace, a new structural shift is underway. This revolution is not occurring on trading floors, but within the essential infrastructure that supports capital markets.

Historically, investment banks managed their own post-trade operations, such as settlements and regulatory reporting, within the Square Mile. This model, once seen as a sign of control, is now becoming unsustainable due to the increasing complexity of global financial markets.

The current infrastructure, built over decades and often customized through acquisitions, is struggling to keep pace with modern demands, particularly the integration of artificial intelligence. AI functions best in well-governed environments, which many banks' legacy systems cannot adequately provide.

In response, capital markets are moving towards what is being called 'Big Bang 2.0.' Instead of owning all infrastructure independently, banks are collaborating to create shared systems, similar to co-working spaces for technology. This approach aims to lower operational complexity and make fixed costs more variable, mirroring trends seen in the broader technology industry.

This shift is blurring the lines between internal bank operations and external service providers, with some banks already outsourcing their over-the-counter derivatives post-trade work. The future of investment banking will rely on this invisible infrastructure, promising a more seamless operation of capital markets.

attribution.originalTitle: 40 years on, the next Big Bang is happening behind the scenes instead of on the trading floor

articles.headline: Plus500 Launches Super-App in US Market

In the first half of 2026, Plus500 reported its highest customer income growth in five years, largely attributed to its expansion in the US. The company has a history of delivering strong returns to investors since its 2013 IPO, with total shareholder returns exceeding $3.1 billion following a recent buyback. Company CEO David Zruia has previously expressed that US exchanges could offer higher valuations for Plus500, noting that the company is valued as a financial services firm rather than a technology company, despite its technological operations. The launch of the super-app aims to bolster Plus500's perception as a tech firm and compete with players like Robinhood in the US investment market.

articles.headline: Heathrow’s third runway is a bottomless money pit. Stop it now | Simon Jenkins
articles.dek: It won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money. The only winner will be the airport’s owners Infrastructure sends politicians berserk.
articles.lead: It won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money. The only winner will be the airport’s owners Infrastructure sends politicians berserk.
articles.takeaway: It won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money.
body: It won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money. The only winner will be the airport’s owners Infrastructure sends politicians berserk.

Propose more money for the health service or reopening youth clubs and frowns break out all round. Can we afford it? But shout infrastructure and cheers go up. The word suggests glamour, chest-beating and “growth”.
Reason flies out of the window. The saga of Heathrow’s third runway beggars belief. A foreign-owned private company wants to make more money out of its cramped west London investment.

The airlines are sceptical and passengers will have to pay surcharges higher than any in Europe. Meanwhile fields lie empty round its rival, Gatwick, and capacity at London’s third airport, Stansted, is underused.
The third runway is a nightmare. The official price tag is now a staggering £49bn but the overall budget for Heathrow’s expansion and operating expenditure could soar beyond £100bn.
An unknown proportion of this will fall on the taxpayer. The proposal has been debated for 20 years and the opening constantly postponed. A date of 2035 has now become 2039.

articles.headline: Government to Curb Non-Compete Clauses, Firms Eye Gardening Leave
articles.dek: New legislation aims to free up the jobs market, but legal experts anticipate businesses will shift to other restrictive employment practices like gardening leave.
articles.lead: The government has announced plans to legislate against the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts, a move intended to stimulate the jobs market for highly skilled workers. Andy Burnham stated that some clauses have "gone too far" and that the legislation will also address lengthy notice periods.
articles.takeaway: New legislation aims to free up the jobs market, but legal experts anticipate businesses will shift to other restrictive employment practices like gardening leave.
body: The government has announced plans to legislate against the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts, a move intended to stimulate the jobs market for highly skilled workers. Andy Burnham stated that some clauses have "gone too far" and that the legislation will also address lengthy notice periods.

In sectors such as technology, finance, and insurance, non-compete clauses are common due to the specialized skills and intellectual property involved. While employees may welcome the change, some businesses in the City express concern about retaining staff and proprietary information.

City lawyers have been preparing for this shift, advising clients on alternative strategies. Experts suggest that companies may increase their reliance on gardening leave, a practice where employees remain on payroll during their notice period but are instructed not to work or contact colleagues.

This development comes as businesses are already navigating significant changes to UK employment laws. The government's move follows a consultation on restrictions for non-compete clauses, with feedback closing earlier this year.

Alternatives to non-compete clauses being considered by firms include financial incentives to retain staff and restructuring bonus payments. Legal professionals anticipate that while the government may seek to limit long notice periods, employers will continue to find ways to manage employee transitions to competitors.

attribution.originalTitle: Banning non-competes is a hollow victory — firms will just ramp up gardening leave

faqs.answer: Businesses are expected to increase their use of gardening leave, financial incentives, and potentially restructure bonus payments to retain staff and protect their interests.
